enrichment.short_title: Partnership property or beneficial joint tenancy on partner's death

statutes_considered.title: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975

key_facts: Michael Bathurst and Philip Scarborow were partners in Southern Darts & Trophies with no written partnership agreement.
In 2000 they bought a house from Mrs Smitherman partly to store partnership stock, financed largely through partnership funds and a partnership bank loan.
The transfer declared beneficial joint tenancy and their solicitor confirmed survivorship would pass the whole property to the survivor.
After Bathurst drowned in 2001, his estate claimed the house was partnership property held in common; Scarborow claimed survivorship as joint tenant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Master Bowman's decision that the house was partnership property and not subject to right of survivorship.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; house declared to belong to Scarborow as surviving beneficial joint tenant; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Partners may agree contrary to the usual presumption that partnership property is held in common; clear evidence of instructions and advice to hold as beneficial joint tenants, with knowledge of survivorship, prevails over the partnership presumption even where the property remains partnership property as between the partners and creditors.
legal_issues: Whether the house was partnership property
Whether the partners agreed to beneficial joint tenancy with right of survivorship
Effect of unsigned transfer form and solicitor's letter
Whether presumption against survivorship in partnership defeats express agreement

enrichment.short_title: Refusal to amend claim to add tort of conspiracy against daughter and solicitor
key_facts: Michael Collier sued solicitors Blount Petrie Kramer after losing to his daughter Diane over Clapham and Empire Bingo Club properties.

notes: Continuing guarantee construction under ICS principles; factual matrix clearly supports whole-debt reading.

enrichment.short_title: Construction of continuing guarantee covering pre-existing trade debt
key_facts: Paul Egan, a director of TBS Cygma PLC, signed successive personal guarantees for Static Control Components.
On 2 September 1999 he signed a continuing guarantee capped at £150,000 after TBS owed about £143,000.
TBS entered administrative receivership in May 2000 owing Static Control £111,883.82, mostly for goods supplied before September 1999.
Egan argued the new guarantee covered only future supplies; Static Control contended it secured the whole debt.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Oldham County Court judgment holding the guarantor liable for the full outstanding debt.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; guarantee construed to cover existing and future debt up to £150,000.
enrichment.ratio: Applying Investors Compensation Scheme principles, a continuing guarantee signed when substantial debt already existed and the limit was doubled should be read to cover the whole debt where business commonsense and the factual matrix show the parties intended increased security for existing and future liabilities, even if literal wording suggests future supplies only.
legal_issues: Whether guarantee words 'you may supply' limit liability to future goods
Role of 'in respect of the whole debt' wording and subrogation point
Application of ICS v West Bromwich to guarantees
Whether contra proferentem applies

enrichment.short_title: Local authority support for unlawfully present mother of British child

statutes_considered.title: Withholding and Withdrawal of Support (Travel Assistance and Temporary Accommodation) Regulations 2002

key_facts: Mrs M, a Guyanese national unlawfully in the UK, cared for her British-born daughter in Islington.
Islington assessed the child as in need and offered one-way tickets to Guyana under section 17, later relying on Schedule 3 restrictions.
Wilson J quashed the travel offer for flawed assessment but held short-term accommodation under the Regulations was permitted.
The appeal concerned whether Schedule 3 and guidance allowed longer accommodation pending immigration appeals.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review quashing Islington's travel offer and remitting welfare assessment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; declaration that Islington has power under Schedule 3 to provide accommodation pending non-cooperation with removal directions; case remitted for reconsideration.
enrichment.ratio: Where a person unlawfully in the UK has a dependant child, local authorities may provide accommodation under Regulation 3(3) for longer than the short periods in guidance when no travel arrangements exist and removal is distant; Convention rights under Schedule 3 paragraph 3 may require Children Act support where Schedule 3 arrangements would breach Article 8.
legal_issues: Effect of Schedule 3 on section 17 support for adults unlawfully present
Scope of temporary accommodation power under Regulation 3(3)
Whether Secretary of State guidance limits accommodation to 10 days
Impact of child's British citizenship and Article 8 rights

enrichment.short_title: When amended pleadings are 'made' for Limitation Act section 35
key_facts: Natasha Furini sued over forged transfers of eight properties from her father Dr Khan's estate.
A Tomlin order consolidated rectification proceedings with an account action against nephew Abdul Bajwa.
The judge permitted amendments in principle on 13 December 2002 but adjourned for revised wording; formal order followed on 9 May 2003.
Bajwa argued a new constructive trust/fraud claim was statute-barred under section 35.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on construction of Tomlin order and whether limitation barred late amendments.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on limitation; amendments treated as made on 9 May 2003 not December 2002; matter remitted to master; Tomlin construction upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 35(3) the relevant date is when amendments are actually made; a judgment approving amendments in principle but adjourning for agreed wording does not constitute making the amendments, so a new cause of action discovered to be time-barred cannot be introduced when the formal order is later entered.
legal_issues: Construction of Tomlin order preserving rectification claims
Whether amendments were 'actually made' on judgment day or order date
Application of section 35 to new cause of action for constructive trust
Effect of Paragon Finance v Thakerar

enrichment.short_title: Freehold ownership dispute between estate and company in liquidation
key_facts: Stephen Dean bought the freehold of 18 Queensgate Place in 1968 while his company Inglorest was in members' voluntary liquidation.
Inglorest claimed an oral contract or resulting trust, relying on spreadsheets showing a £9,550 purchase from Dean.
Dean registered the freehold in his own name; after his 1983 death litigation among beneficiaries lasted years.
Liquidator and advisers later accepted the freehold belonged to Dean's estate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against declaration that freehold formed part of Dean's estate and dismissal of Inglorest's counterclaim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; freehold held part of Dean's estate; caution cancelled.
enrichment.ratio: On the evidence Dean purchased the freehold with funds debited to his personal account with the company, not as a company purchase; insufficient proof of oral contract, part performance or constructive trust overcomes section 40 and registered title after decades of inconsistent treatment.

enrichment.short_title: Disability living allowance appeals and supersession challenge refused
key_facts: Mr Farrington had long-running disputes over disability living allowance dating from 1996.
A tribunal awarded the lowest care component from April 1998 to April 2003 and he purportedly withdrew an earlier appeal.
Commissioner Angus upheld the DLA award and held a supersession appeal had lapsed after an earlier commissioner decision quashed the underlying decision.
Farrington sought permission to appeal and to judicial review the refusal to challenge his withdrawal of an appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for permission to appeal commissioner decisions and for permission to appeal refusal of judicial review.
enrichment.outcome: Applications dismissed; no permission to appeal; no order for costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where a commissioner has quashed the decision superseded, there is nothing left to appeal against the supersession; tribunal fact-finding on the care component disclosed no error of law; judicial review of withdrawal was out of time and would fail on merits.

Whether tribunal misapplied DLA care component regulations

enrichment.short_title: Tax inspector unfair dismissal: non-disclosure of retirement age change
key_facts: Mr Scott, a senior Inland Revenue inspector, was unfairly dismissed and discriminated against after a mishandled sexual harassment complaint.
The tribunal awarded compensation including injury to feelings and psychiatric harm but refused costs.
The Inland Revenue changed retirement policy in 2002 to allow working to 65 but did not disclose it during remedies.
Scott's loss calculations had assumed compulsory retirement at 60.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to Court of Appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal on compensation, disclosure and costs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; case remitted on psychiatric damages and costs; retirement-to-65 issue may be raised on remittal; respondent ordered to pay costs.
enrichment.ratio: A party must disclose documents affecting compensation while proceedings are undetermined; failure to disclose a new retirement policy materially affecting loss was an error; psychiatric award was too low due to misreading medical evidence; costs decision must be reconsidered applying the 'misconceived' conduct threshold.

Whether retirement policy change affected loss calculation
Adequacy of injury to feelings and psychiatric damage awards

enrichment.short_title: Section 34 adverse inference from silence despite solicitor's advice

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Kevin Hoare ran a large-scale amphetamine production operation at a Sussex farm from 1998 to 2002.
Graham Pierce conspired to supply amphetamine; he received a box from Hoare containing cut drug shortly before arrest.
Both remained silent in police interview on solicitors' advice and gave innocent explanations at trial.
Hoare was sentenced to 12 years; Pierce to 10 years for conspiracy to supply.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction and renewed application for leave to appeal against sentence after trial at Lewes Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals against conviction dismissed; applications for leave to appeal against sentence refused.
enrichment.ratio: Summary evidence of no-comment interviews can suffice for a section 34 direction where questioning plainly sought to discover whether offences were committed; genuine reliance on legal advice to remain silent does not automatically preclude adverse inference if the true reason for silence was absence of an innocent explanation consistent with the facts relied on at trial.
legal_issues: Sufficiency of summary interview evidence for section 34 direction
Objective versus subjective test for reliance on solicitor's advice
Whether detention made Pierce's interview inadmissible
Fairness of non-disclosure about uniqueness of manufacturing process
